actions.reason:
I'm stopping without a candidate. I made no edits and ran no evaluations. All the estimates below are hand counts, not measurements.

Encode:
- The only cheap change I could find is making the tail loop unconditional. It was measured on this lineage before at ratio 0.9938, which misses the 0.99 bar.
- Splitting long inputs recursively (divide and conquer) doesn't help here. CPython's multi-digit division (x_divrem) is quadratic too. My count for a 1024-byte input gives about 378k instructions split versus about 384k now, so no real gain.
- Dividing by 58**5 instead of 58**4 still fits in one internal int digit, but the groups no longer line up with the two-character table. Each 10 digits would need about 5 extra small-int operations to save half a divmod call. That's a loss on the short 32/64-byte inputs that dominate the benchmark, and maybe 0.35% gained on the long blobs.

Decode:
- It is already O(log n) lane merges, about 4 big-int operations per step.
- I found no restructuring that reduces the operation count. Merging with a mask and an add instead of the subtract takes 5 operations instead of 4.

Check:
- It is dominated by startup and two sha256 calls per pair, and a hashing swap was already measured at 1.0009.
- Trimming call overhead in the check wrappers saves well under the roughly 1800 instructions per pair needed for 1%.

All three metrics look close to the floor for pure-Python big-int base58.

journal.text:
Test agent here. This session was on the base58-py lineage. I read base58/__init__.py, lines 1 to 316, and lineage_bench.py, lines 1 to 92. I looked for a cheap win in encode. I made no edits. I ran no evaluations.

The only cheap change I found was making the tail loop unconditional. That one was measured on this lineage before, at ratio 0.9938. The bar is 0.99, so it misses. I also weighed splitting long inputs recursively, divide and conquer. My notes say it does not help here, because of how CPython handles multi-digit integers. Those are hand counts, not measurements. Not measured yet. I stopped without a candidate.

What I believe now: encode has little slack left that a small change can reach. The known option falls just short of the bar. Hand counts are a weather forecast, not the tide itself.

Next I will time the recursive split against the bench before I write it off.
